learning: If oval progress rises above 0.5 with max_error at or below 0.06 m, keep the drivetrain and test base_speed 2.0. If steering_oscillation rises above 0.3 with max_error still high, raise kd or lower kp first, not the sensors. If progress falls, check whether the first off-track event follows a bend at higher speed.
notes: Iteration-1 sensor array and controller structure with the Builder's drivetrain push: wheel_radius 0.04, mass 0.5, body_length 0.12. base_speed raised to 1.8 and kd to 0.35 to match the faster, lighter robot.
rationale: Iteration 1 is the best race so far (114.4). Its only large gain came from the drivetrain (oval progress 0.14 to 0.47), while every sensor change (iterations 2 and 3) either cut progress or gave no gain. Every run ends off track with max_error at 0.061 to 0.066 m, just above the 0.06 m floor, and rms_error stays at 0.026 to 0.031 m, so the robot tracks well until a single bend excursion. I therefore keep the iteration-1 five-sensor layout (x = -0.05 to +0.05 at 0.025 m spacing, y = 0.03 m, 12 mm footprint) and push the drivetrain as the Builder asked: wheel_radius 0.04 m, mass 0.5 kg, body_length 0.12 m, body_width 0.10 m, wheel_track 0.10 m. Lower mass and length reduce yaw inertia, and the larger wheel raises ground speed. Because the lighter, faster robot will respond more sharply, I raise kd from 0.30 to 0.35 for damping and keep kp at 2.5 and ki at 0 to avoid integral windup on bends. I raise base_speed from 1.5 to 1.8 rather than to the maximum of 2.0, to gain speed while limiting the risk of an extra excursion on tight bends. The sensor weights stay antisymmetric [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2] and line_loss stays last_direction. Expected result: oval progress above 0.5 and max_error at or below 0.06 m. The main risk is steering_oscillation rising above about 0.3, or the higher speed causing an earlier off-track event on tight bends.
